readerTitle: Your best work is no longer your job
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (금속 부품 공장, 소프트웨어 회사) + 실제 연구 (Wasserman 2008, Grove 1983)
insight: 회사가 커지면 창업자의 성과는 자기가 한 일이 아니라 팀이 해낸 일로 측정된다. 일을 잘하는 사람에서 일이 되게 하는 사람으로 바뀌어야 한다.
misconception: 창업자가 모든 결정과 핵심 업무를 직접 챙겨야 품질이 유지된다. 가장 열심히 일하면 회사도 가장 빨리 자란다.

sources.text: Grove, A. (1983). High Output Management. Random House. (관리자의 산출물 = 그가 이끄는 조직의 산출물)
Wasserman, N. (2008). The Founder's Dilemma. Harvard Business Review, February 2008.
공장·소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Wasserman(2008) HBR 기사의 수치 확인 필요: 미국 스타트업 212곳 분석, 창업 3년 차에 약 50%의 창업자가 CEO가 아니었고, IPO까지 CEO로 남은 창업자는 4분의 1 미만. 카드에는 "about half", "fewer than a quarter"로 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 대조 필요.
Grove의 "a manager's output is the output of the organization" 문장은 High Output Management의 핵심 명제로 의역해 인용했습니다. 직접 인용 부호는 쓰지 않았습니다. 원문 표현 확인 권장.
가상 사례 수치(직원 45명·40명, 견적 대기 1주, 주 70시간, 견적 한도 $20,000)는 모두 설명용입니다.

cards.title: Your best work is no longer your job
body: Two founders. One runs a metal parts factory. The other runs a software company. Each has about 40 people, and each works 70 hours a week.
Both are the most skilled person in their building. And in both companies, that has quietly become the problem.

image.label: Two founders at desks buried under waiting paperwork
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 화면을 반으로 나눠 왼쪽은 공장 사무실(기계 부품, 견적서 더미), 오른쪽은 소프트웨어 사무실(노트북, 코드 리뷰 알림). 두 창업자 모두 책상 앞에 앉아 있고, 뒤에 직원들이 서류나 노트북을 들고 줄 서서 기다림. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Every quote waits for Maria.
body: Maria founded a 45-person shop that makes custom metal parts. She knows pricing better than anyone, so she writes every customer quote herself.
Quotes now take a week. Some customers are ordering elsewhere. What should she do?

options.text: Work evenings and weekends until the backlog clears
options.feedback: The backlog shrinks this month, but the bottleneck stays. As orders grow, it comes back bigger, and Maria has nothing left to give.

options.text: Hire an assistant to draft quotes that she then approves
options.feedback: It saves typing time. But every quote still needs Maria's yes, so the queue moves only a little faster.

options.text: Teach two staff her pricing rules, let them send quotes up to a set size, and check a sample each week
options.feedback: She gives up some control over each quote and gains a company that quotes without her. Her weekly check keeps quality in view.

cards.title: Sam has the same problem in a different outfit.
body: Sam founded a 40-person software company. He still reviews every code change before release and joins most sales calls.
His engineers wait days for his review. Deals stall when he's busy. Like Maria, he isn't doing bad work. He's doing good work that everyone else has to wait for.
Two industries, one pattern: the founder is the **bottleneck**, the narrow point everything must pass through.

image.label: An hourglass with the founder at the narrow middle
image.brief: 모래시계 일러스트. 위쪽에 주문서, 견적, 코드 변경, 영업 미팅 아이콘이 가득 쌓여 있고, 가운데 좁은 목 부분에 작은 창업자 캐릭터가 서 있음. 아래쪽으로는 아주 조금만 흘러내림.

cards.title: From founder to CEO
body: Early on, a founder's job is to **do the work**: make the product, close the sale, fix the machine.
As the company grows, the job changes. A CEO's job is to build the team and the system that do the work, and to decide what matters most.

Andy Grove, who led Intel, put it simply in *High Output Management*: a manager's output is the output of the organization they lead. Your personal work counts only through what it makes possible for others.

cards.title: Four shifts in what you do all day.
body: The change isn't one decision. It's a set of habits that move slowly.
list: **From doing** the work to choosing who does it
**From answering** every question to writing rules so others can answer
**From being the best performer** to coaching others toward your standard
**From checking everything** to knowing which few things to check
cards.callout: A good test: what still happens when you're away for a week?
cards.softwareNote: In a software company this often means moving from reviewing code to setting review standards, from closing deals to hiring and coaching a sales lead, and from owning the roadmap alone to running a clear process for deciding it.

cards.title: Many founders don't make the switch.
body: Noam Wasserman studied 212 American startups for a 2008 *Harvard Business Review* article. By year three, about half of the founders were no longer CEO. Fewer than a quarter were still CEO when their company went public.

Many were replaced not because they failed, but because the company outgrew the job they were doing. The skills that build a product are not the same as the skills that build an organization. Some founders learn the new job. Others choose to hand it over.

cards.title: Letting go is not disappearing.
body: Some decisions stay with the CEO: direction, key hires, how cash is spent, and what the company will not do. Handing those off is not delegation. It's leaving.
Timing matters too. If you delegate work you've never done yourself, you can't tell good results from bad. Most founders need to do a job first, then teach it.
And the shift costs something real. Quality may dip while others learn. That dip is the price of a company that can grow past one person.

cards.title: Back to Sam's software company.
body: Releases slip because every code change waits for Sam's review. Two senior engineers have been with him for three years. What's his best next step?

options.text: Stop reviewing code entirely so the team can move fast
options.feedback: Speed comes back at once, but no one has agreed what good looks like. Quality can slide before anyone notices.

options.text: Write down his review standards, make the two seniors reviewers, and spot-check a few changes each week
options.feedback: He trades personal control of every change for a team that can judge quality itself. The spot-checks tell him if the standard holds.

options.text: Keep reviewing, but only on weekends to stay out of the way
options.feedback: It may ease weekday pressure, but releases still wait for Sam, and he burns out faster.

cards.title: Measure yourself by what your team gets done.
body: As your business grows, your job moves from doing the best work to building a team that does it without you.
**Try it today:** list three things that wait for your approval. For one of them, write the rule you use to decide, and hand it to someone you trust.
